children: Hyundai Motor India’s AVP & Vertical Head, People Strategy, on future skills, role-based careers, women leaders, employee experience and the evolving role of HR

As technology, business models and workforce expectations continue to evolve, organisations are increasingly rethinking how they build skills, structure roles and prepare their people for the future. At Hyundai Motor India Limited (HMIL), this has involved a shift towards a role-based organisation, a capability architecture that balances current and future requirements, and greater emphasis on internal talent development and mobility.

In an interaction with BW People, Dr Natwar Kadel, AVP & Vertical Head, People Strategy, Hyundai Motor India Limited, discusses how the company is preparing its workforce for changing business needs, redesigning career progression, developing women leaders and creating a more personalised employee experience. He also shares why he believes HR must move beyond its traditional perception as a support function and become directly accountable for business outcomes, capability building and organisational transformation.

The shelf life of skills is becoming shorter as technology and business models evolve. How is Hyundai Motor India identifying the capabilities it will need three to five years from now, rather than simply responding to today's skill gaps?

We are an organisation with a clear focus on what we want to deliver in the next five years, but that five-year plan keeps changing every year. You cannot have a five-year plan and sit still thinking that you need to follow it exactly. The plan is extremely dynamic because what we were yesterday, we are not going to be the same tomorrow.
While having a clear vision of where we want to be five years from now, we are integrating the skill requirements into our systems and workplace. The objective is to build the workforce for tomorrow.
We have brought 2030 into our vision and are building those skills today. We infuse multi-skilling and the need for upskilling across the workforce — from the shop floor to specialists and leaders.

The shelf life of skills has reduced significantly. What we used to see as a skill having a shelf life of around 35 years about seven decades ago has reduced to less than two years today. The skill required today will not necessarily remain relevant throughout one's career.

We have therefore defined a capability architecture that looks at both behavioural and functional elements. We focus 60 per cent on the context of today, while infusing 40 per cent of the requirement for the future. That future keeps evolving every year based on what we learn and what needs to be incorporated into our capability design.
The objective is to remain ahead of the curve so that when things unfold, we are ready for them.

You have been instrumental in driving HMIL’s digital HR transformation and role-based organisational model. How has this changed the way Hyundai defines roles, career paths and talent mobility within the organisation?
In 2023, we paused and thought that if we continued working in the same way, our systems and processes would not cater to changing business requirements.

The first step was to become a role-based organisation. I do not have 10,000 job descriptions; all I have is 450 unique roles where people are being clustered to roles. We then defined our capability framework to understand what those roles require from a behavioural and functional perspective.The next part was making the organisation design dynamic. We are not going to have an organisation structure that remains unchanged for years. We change it every year and, where required, even within the year.

We are designing the structures we will need for the business over the next five years and building that talent today. Performance and career architecture are also changing. We are looking at continuous improvement, Objectives and Key Results (OKRs), transparent performance scales and constant check-ins.

We are no more an organisation which does the promotion for every three years. A promotion can happen in a year or later. What matters is that you are bringing a change to your role. You need to grow horizontally to be eligible to grow vertically.Digital transformation enables us to connect the entire employee journey, from the time a person enters the organisation until retirement, around these 450 roles.

We have transformed from 15 layers of designation to a five-layer responsibility structure. We spent around 60 to 80 per cent of our time explaining the change before implementing it because people have to buy into what you aspire to and what you envision.We transformed into a role-based organisation in nine months. But that is not the end. We aspire to become a skill-based organisation, cutting down further layers, becoming more skill-driven and building an organisation that is future-proof.

You have also worked on leadership development, women in leadership and career advancement for high-potential talent. What are the biggest barriers that still prevent high-potential employees — particularly women — from moving into leadership roles?

A high-potential employee is not just a subject-matter specialist. We look at sustained performance along with the potential to perform tomorrow. We look at whether someone can perform different jobs, extend their capabilities, operate at scale and deliver in an extremely complex scenario.

At Hyundai, our high-potential programmes are connected with leadership development and succession. We identify talent from top schools and engineering institutions, develop them over three years and then provide further opportunities through high-potential programmes. These programmes are also extended to laterals who reach the required level.

With our role-based organisation, the pace of career progression can be faster. We are looking at people potentially moving to VP-level roles within 15 years, and someone could even become a CEO in less than 20 years.
When it comes to women, we realised that our diversity numbers were not where we wanted them to be. We therefore took a series of steps through what we call our women-at-work architecture.
We did not just look at numbers. We looked at roles, opportunities, policies, platforms, processes, exposure, education and experience.

One of these initiatives is Trailblazer, our exclusive women’s leadership development programme. It is a one-year development programme with XLRI as an education partner. Participants visit manufacturing partners and organisations in the supply chain, work with coaches and receive stretch and challenging assignments.
We have completed one batch and moved to the second. We have seen successful stories, with women who completed the programme taking on leadership responsibilities at different levels.

I would not say that systems or processes are the biggest hurdle. The biggest hurdle in anyone’s development today is your own self. If you are not preparing yourself to make a difference tomorrow, you are creating a hurdle for yourself.

Hyundai has been recognised as a Top Employer for three consecutive years. What are the people practices behind that recognition that you believe have had the most tangible impact on employee experience and organisational performance?

Hyundai has always been different in what it can do for its people. From our Managing Director to our Executive Chair of the Group and every leader today, we have a similar opinion and we echo the same thought: employees are central to whatever we do.

We understand why people are important. We have seen tremendous growth over the last 30 years, and we clearly believe that the factor that has made the difference is our people. These people will take us much further over the next 30 years.Our practices and policies are not aligned only to today; they are aligned to tomorrow. They are not designed around one generation but around diverse populations across India. We have a workforce across the country, and we cater to different needs. Inclusivity is something we firmly believe in.

We have an employee-centric culture and a strong focus on learning and development. Growth and career growth are extremely important to us, but we rely heavily on internal growth. Ninety per cent of our leaders are home-grown.We are also bringing digital fluency into everything we do, whether in human capital or other functions. We want leadership to be accessible. Our leaders practise open and friendly communication, because being with employees is extremely important.

Employee wellbeing is also central to us. Our framework around physical and social wellness is an important part of our approach, alongside our benefits.We want employees not just to come home smiling but also to go back smiling. That creates organisational pride.

When it comes to the workplace, we want to create a safe environment where people love working. Are our Mondays already feeling like Fridays? I think we will always strive for perfection, but we are committed to becoming better every day.The most important thing is consistency in our practices across the employee lifecycle. We learn from the world, from ourselves and from our people. Our intent is to be different from what we were yesterday and create a happy workplace.

With employee expectations changing across generations, how do you create a workplace that offers flexibility and personalisation while maintaining a consistent culture, performance standards and business priorities?
We firmly believe that the Hyundai Way defines who we are. Values and culture cannot change or be tailor-made from one person to another because, at the end, we are all recognised as Hyundai.

What changes is the experience we offer employees. It is extremely tailor-made today.My approach towards the plant, manufacturing, quality and safety is very different from what I do at headquarters, sales, service or product strategy. The need is different because we are not just a role-based organisation for the sake of doing it. We understand that needs are different according to roles, aspirations, work and the stage of the business where people operate.

It is therefore important to give employees a customised and tailor-made experience. Our employee experience design is created to ensure that everyone is part of the same journey but still feels that we have connected with them emotionally where required.We have adapted to become a flexible organisation and provide some degree of flexibility to employees. But policies and practices cannot simply be cut, copied and pasted from another organisation. They have to be tailor-made for what works for you.
We need to understand what our people want, what our business wants and what will deliver the best for our customers.

After more than two decades in people leadership, what is one assumption about HR that you think businesses still get wrong — and what should the modern CHRO or People leader actually be accountable for?

One myth is that HR is a support function. That itself is wrong.HR is the spine of an organisation and brings immense value because we are business enablers. We understand what each function wants. Our existence depends on their existence. If we do not cater to them, we become obsolete and can become a factor in the damage that happens to the business.

It is therefore important for us to be ahead of the curve — to build and stitch together the structure, processes, people, talent and organisation so that they are ready for what comes next.Talent is becoming increasingly dynamic. The definition of talent changes with time, and capability building and future workforce readiness are extremely important.

Before talent comes to your organisation, you need to be able to tell them what is in it for them. Unless you can sell that proposition, talent will not come to your organisation.One of the biggest concerns for organisations is building leaders for tomorrow. Leadership development has to be deeply infused into everything we do because building leadership is about building businesses.

We are also trying to drive organisational agility and transformation. The transformation architecture we designed in 2023 may not work in 2027, so we are already working on the architecture that will work towards 2030.We are leveraging technology and data for better people decisions. Most importantly, we are defining our people strategy around the business strategy and making it an important ingredient for business success.

We are instilling accountability for culture, capability, productivity and business outcomes. We are measuring success through the business impact created through people.Products and processes will continue to evolve and make a difference, as they have over the last 30 years. But we should never undermine the fact that it is people who brought about that difference.
